article.title: Kitesurf is now open source | Cloudflare Blog
article.text:
Open SourceRustWebAssemblyWorkers
AgentsAIBrowser RunOpen SourceRustWebAssemblyWorkers
November 13, 2026
Kitesurf is now open source
Celso Martinho, Rui Figueira, Bernardo Pereira, and Luís Duarte
4 minute read
We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.
That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.
A browser built for agents
Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.
Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.
Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.
What is inside the repository?
Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:
Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.
Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.
Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).
Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.
These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.
Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.
All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.
Run your own Kitesurf
To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:
git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run dev
The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.
You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:
import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";
const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});
try {
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto("https://example.com/");
await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });
} finally {
await browser.disconnect();
}
Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
Deploy to your Cloudflare account
When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.
From the repository root:
pnpm run deploy
Help us make it better
As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note…

article.title: An update on our recent security incident · Cursor
article.text:
Blog / company
Nov 13, 2026·company
An update on our recent security incident
6 min read
On October 29, we shared that we were investigating a security incident and a malicious, unauthorized copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension that appeared in the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace. After an extensive investigation over the past two weeks, we want to share more context on the attack and the related impact.
The vast majority of customers were not affected, and we have contacted each affected customer directly with the details that apply to them.
Protecting the safety of our customers' data is a core priority we take seriously. This incident involved data we stored and shared, credentials we issued, and systems we operate. We are addressing the impacts and are enhancing our security measures based on what we have learned.
#What happened
Our investigation has pieced together the following picture:
It started at Fireworks. An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks. The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them. That bucket contained limited coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions not in Privacy Mode, which we were permitted to use for model training. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted; less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. Starting with those credentials, the attacker reached select SaaS tools used by Cursor. From these tools they accessed select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories (some containing business contact information), limited customer support data and email conversations, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding agent conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team.
Our monitoring systems identified the unauthorized activity. After becoming aware of the unauthorized activity, we deactivated the vendor's key, opened an incident response workstream, and began revoking and rotating credentials and hunting for any further unauthorized access. As we identified further access, we cut it off. Out of an abundance of caution, we temporarily disabled internal and product services well beyond what the evidence required, which temporarily disrupted certain Cursor features. We restored each one once it was safe to do so.
The attacker published a malicious extension. On October 29, using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system, the attacker placed malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace. Anthropic did not publish this copy, and this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product. The marketplace source, Open VSX, never had the malware. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build. It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down.
We notified customers. On October 30, we published a security notice on our blog and on X with indicators of compromise, remediation steps and scripts to check your system, and began notifying affected users and team admins through in-app notices and email. If credentials were exposed, we emailed team admins a list of the specific keys to rotate, and asked the third-party services that issued those credentials to revoke them. If customer support or business data may have been involved, we notified customers directly. If customers installed or updated to tampered version Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace during the exposure window, we ask customers to follow the steps in our security notice. article.title: Anthropic's Claude Code Projects get a proactive coordinator, thread sharing and reminders — AI Frontier Post
article.text:
AI News
Anthropic's Claude Code Projects get a proactive coordinator, thread sharing and reminders
Anthropic shipped a second act for Projects in Claude Code on Friday, and the headline change is about who does the checking in. The project's coordinator — the Claude instance that scopes a request, splits it across parallel threads, and stitches the results back together — is now, in Anthropic's words, 'much more proactive': it answers questions directly in the project chat and posts status updates as its threads make progress, instead of waiting to be asked.
PNPriya NairResearch Editor · November 14, 2026 · 6 min read
TL;DR: Anthropic upgraded Projects in Claude Code on November 13: the coordinator now reports in the project chat instead of waiting to be polled, /btw and /fork split work into side threads, threads can be shared as read-only links, and reminders park a thread until you need it. Projects remain in public beta on Pro and Max, with a waitlist for everyone else.
The announcement: a thread from Anthropic's ClaudeDevs account on X, posted at 5:51 p.m. ET on November 13, 2026 — 525,000 views, 10,000 likes and 647 reposts within hours.
The headline change: the project coordinator is now proactive: it answers questions in the project chat and posts status updates on its running threads, instead of waiting to be asked.
New commands: /btw moves a tangent into its own thread so the current one stays on topic; /fork starts a new thread from the current one to try a different approach.
Reminders and sharing: set a reminder on any thread, or ask Claude to remind you; share an individual thread as a read-only link with anyone signed in to Claude — except threads that had access to your computer, which cannot be shared.
Availability: public beta on Pro and Max plans, with a waitlist for subscribers without access; Team and Enterprise plans come later.
Illustration: one project chat fanning out into parallel coding threads. AI-generated editorial illustration for AI Frontier Post.

The update, announced by Anthropic's ClaudeDevs account on X on November 13, also adds /btw and /fork commands for spinning off side threads, reminders that park a thread until a set time, read-only sharing links for individual threads, and a tidier threads panel with artifact thumbnails. The announcement post passed 525,000 views and 10,000 likes overnight — a strong reception for what is, on its face, a workflow polish release rather than a new model. That is the point: the most-used coding harness is now selling multi-agent coordination as a default, not a demo.
What changed on November 13#
The announcement was a six-post thread. In brief:
A more active coordinator. It answers questions in the project chat and gives updates on the status of ongoing threads.
/btw and /fork. /btw moves a new topic to its own thread so the current one stays on topic; /fork starts a new thread from the current one to try a different approach.
Reminders. Set a reminder on any thread, or ask Claude to remind you. The thread moves out of the way until then, then returns and Claude raises it in the project chat.
Thread sharing. Share an individual thread as a read-only link with anyone signed in to Claude, from the thread menu. Threads that had access to your computer cannot be shared.
Artifacts are easier to find. The threads panel has a top row of recently opened, updated, or pinned threads, and each thread shows thumbnails of its artifacts, which can be turned off in view settings.

article.title: Advancing science & engineering with Antigravity’s /teamwork
article.text:
Advancing science & engineering with Antigravity’s /teamwork
November 13, 2026
Vahab Mirrokni, Google Fellow and VP, Google Research
We share recent results from Antigravity’s /teamwork multiagent systems, which enhance human-AI collaborations to solve open problems across mathematics, chemistry, systems software, and ML engineering. All of this work is done in collaboration with human experts, and we are making these tools available externally.
Quick links
Antigravity blog
Gemini 4 Argon
Antigravity Teamwork
Researcher access program
×
Over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years. Using Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and multi-agent workflows such as Antigravity’s /teamwork (building on various Gemini models), these collaborations have produced new innovations across information theory, formal verifications, molecular structure discoveries, and kernel optimization, along with several production infrastructure gains at Google. We are making these agentic tools available in Antigravity’s /teamwork (alongside /boost and other agents) so that researchers and developers can apply them to their own work.
Frontier research and systems engineering require navigating vast literature, building custom computational pipelines, testing against physical measurements, and verifying every step. Progress comes from an interactive discovery loop where researchers frame questions and define the theoretical or physical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, explore large search spaces, test candidate designs, and check long chains of logic.
Scaling long-horizon reasoning
Two limits of current language models motivate /teamwork's design. First, model generation can be unpredictable, leaving a gap between a single attempt and finding the correct answer. The system bridges this gap by pairing parallel exploration with dedicated falsifiers (e.g., the Lean 4 proof checker, unmodified software test suites, execution simulators, web search, or hardware counters) to automatically verify which candidate solutions work.
Second, AI models often lose track of details over multi-day tasks because attention disperses across growing context windows. To prevent this, /teamwork partitions context by construction: each specialized agent receives only the exact files and tools it needs for a specific step. Coordinators hand off tasks to fresh successors, while critics and auditors challenge and verify results from clean contexts without the original producer's reasoning.
Teamwork expresses these workflows as declarative self-improving natural-language patterns and dynamically routes each user prompt to the pattern best suited to the task. These patterns range from distributed coding and iterative problem-solving (packaged standalone as /boost, a sequential solve-and-verify loop refined from prior trajectories) to specialized research workflows like long proof and document review, all of which are available in Antigravity today. This allows teams to design custom specifications from past run transcripts routing across different harness patterns and dynamically improving agentic harness. While many of these features are available in Antigravity, we will provide more updates in the coming weeks providing all the features to our external users on Antigravity. Following our previous posts on Antigravity /teamwork, we provide new results to open challenges empowered by new variants of /teamwork and Gemini 4 models.
Mathematics and theoretical computer science
Across mathematics and theoretical computer science, researchers paired with Gemini 4 and /teamwork harnesses to collaborate on large-scale proofs and generate complete algorithms and proofs directly from open problem statements. We present several examples.
